def: A Bernoulli trial is a random experiment with exactly two possible outcomes, usually called 'success' and 'failure'. A sequence of such trials is called Bernoulli trials when certain conditions are met.
points: Each trial has only two outcomes: success (probability p) or failure (probability q), with p + q = 1.
The number of trials, n, is fixed in advance.
The trials are independent: the outcome of one trial does not affect another.
The probability of success p remains the same in every trial.
Examples: tossing a coin repeatedly, checking defective items from a production line.
These conditions must all hold for the Binomial Distribution to apply.
formula: p + q = 1, where p = probability of success, q = probability of failure

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Fixed number of trials n"] --> E["Bernoulli Trials"]
  B["Only two outcomes"] --> E
  C["Independent trials"] --> E
  D["Constant probability p"] --> E

example: Tossing a fair coin 5 times: each toss has 2 outcomes (head/tail), p = 0.5 stays same, trials are independent, n = 5 is fixed. This satisfies Bernoulli trial conditions.
tip: Always check and state all four conditions explicitly in the answer before applying the binomial formula — this is a direct mark-scoring step.

t: Binomial Probability Mass Function: nCr p^r q^(n-r)
def: The binomial p.m.f. gives the probability of getting exactly r successes in n independent Bernoulli trials, where each trial has success probability p.
points: X follows a binomial distribution, written X ~ B(n, p).
The probability of exactly r successes is P(X = r) = nCr p^r q^(n-r).
nCr = n! / (r! (n-r)!) counts the number of ways to arrange r successes among n trials.
p^r is the probability of r successes, q^(n-r) is the probability of the remaining (n-r) failures.
r can take whole number values from 0 to n.
Sum of P(X=r) for r = 0 to n always equals 1.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Identify n, p, q"] --> B["Choose r successes needed"]
  B --> C["Compute nCr"]
  C --> D["Multiply by p^r and q^(n-r)"]
  D --> E["Get P(X = r)"]

tip: Clearly identify n, p, q, and r first in every problem before substituting into the formula — this avoids mixing up values.

t: Mean (np) and Variance (npq) of Binomial Distribution
def: For a binomial distribution X ~ B(n, p), the mean (expected number of successes) is np, and the variance (spread of the distribution) is npq.
points: Mean of binomial distribution: E(X) = np.
Variance of binomial distribution: Var(X) = npq, where q = 1 - p.
Standard deviation: SD(X) = sqrt(npq).
These formulas are derived using the sum formulas for E(X) and E(X^2) but are usually used directly.
If mean and variance are given, they can be used to find n and p (see later topic).
Variance is always less than or equal to the mean, since npq <= np (because q <= 1).
formula: Mean = np     Variance = npq     SD = sqrt(npq)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Given n and p"] --> B["Mean = n x p"]
  A --> C["q = 1 - p"]
  C --> D["Variance = n x p x q"]
  D --> E["SD = sqrt of variance"]

tip: Memorise mean = np and variance = npq directly — deriving them from scratch in an exam wastes valuable time.

t: Computing Probabilities of a Given Number of Successes
def: This means directly applying the binomial p.m.f. formula to calculate the probability of exactly r successes (or a set of specific values of r) out of n trials.
points: Identify n (number of trials), p (probability of success), and q = 1 - p from the question.
Identify the required value(s) of r (number of successes asked).
Substitute n, p, q, r into P(X = r) = nCr p^r q^(n-r).
Calculate nCr using factorials, then compute p^r and q^(n-r) separately.
Multiply all three parts together to get the final probability.
If asked for more than one value of r, calculate each separately and add if needed (e.g., for 'exactly 2 or exactly 3').

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Identify n, p, q, r"] --> B["Compute nCr"]
  B --> C["Compute p^r"]
  C --> D["Compute q^(n-r)"]
  D --> E["Multiply to get probability"]

example: A die is rolled 3 times; success = getting a 6, so p = 1/6, q = 5/6, n = 3. P(exactly 1 six) = 3C1 (1/6)^1 (5/6)^2 = 3 x (1/6) x (25/36) = 75/216.
tip: Keep fractions unsimplified until the final answer to avoid rounding errors in intermediate steps.

def: At least r successes means r or more successes (X >= r); at most r successes means r or fewer successes (X <= r). These are solved by adding relevant individual binomial probabilities.
points: 'At least r' means P(X >= r) = P(X=r) + P(X=r+1) + ... + P(X=n).
It is often easier to use the complement: P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X < r) = 1 - [P(X=0)+...+P(X=r-1)].
'At most r' means P(X <= r) = P(X=0) + P(X=1) + ... + P(X=r), added directly.
'At least 1 success' is most simply found as P(X >= 1) = 1 - P(X = 0).
Always identify clearly which values of r need to be included before adding.
Double-check by ensuring all probabilities used are correctly computed with the binomial formula first.
formula: P(X >= r) = 1 - P(X < r)     P(X <= r) = sum from 0 to r of P(X=k)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Question asks at least or at most"] --> B["List required r values"]
  B --> C["Use complement if at least r is large"]
  C --> D["Add individual P(X=k) values"]
  D --> E["Get final probability"]

tip: For 'at least 1', always use the shortcut 1 - P(X=0) instead of adding many terms — it saves time and reduces errors.

t: Finding n and p from Mean and Variance
def: When the mean and variance of a binomial distribution are both given, we can find the unknown values of n and p by using the standard formulas mean = np and variance = npq together.
points: Write down the two given equations: np = mean, and npq = variance.
Divide variance by mean: npq / np = q = variance / mean.
This directly gives q, the probability of failure.
Find p using p = 1 - q.
Substitute p back into np = mean to solve for n.
Check that n comes out as a positive whole number, since n must be an integer number of trials.
formula: q = Variance / Mean     p = 1 - q     n = Mean / p

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Given mean np and variance npq"] --> B["Divide variance by mean to get q"]
  B --> C["Find p = 1 - q"]
  C --> D["Substitute into np = mean"]
  D --> E["Solve for n"]

tip: Always verify your final n is a whole number and p is between 0 and 1 — if not, recheck your division in the first step.
